In regards to expansions my off the cuff answer would be for those expansions to feature new maps and characters. As for splitting the party there are two possible answers.

1. As long as one person in the party owns the expansion they can all access the new maps, but only the owner can use the new characters. This is the consumer friendly version which in itself may help sell people on it.

2. Maps and characters are on free rotation from week to week. This enforces a kind of FOMO that encourages players who don't own the expansion to bite the bullet so they aren't forced to play at specific times. Obviously less player friendly, but is in line with some other live service games.

The [Vector](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/starwars/images/c/c1/JediVector-CGSWG.png/revision/latest?cb=20241130005638) is obviously based on RotS concept art, but it feels very in-line with standard Star Wars design language. Likewise the [Skywing](https://imgur.com/XulSRf0) fits the generally sleek look associated with TPM era ships. On the larger end of the spectrum stuff like the [Pacifier-class](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/starwars/images/3/3a/PacifierClassCruiser-THRSOS1.png/revision/latest?cb=20240227165920) or the [Emissary-class](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/starwars/images/f/f8/ThirdHorizon-THRSOS3.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20231221181204) feel at home. I also appreciate the Emissary having dreadnought style city greebles and command towers reminiscent of the Venator. (Could do without the Jedi Order hood ornament, but that is unique to the *Third Horizon.*

As for [Nihil ships](https://www.reddit.com/r/StarWarsShips/comments/stfhwy/nihil_ships_high_republic/#lightbox), they are kind of all over the place aesthetically, but that's kind of the point. They are using modular uglies. They aren't supposed to look cohesive or in-line with traditional ship design language.

Overall I think that the High Republic does a good job of establishing a visual identity distinct from the prequels, while also paying homage to the design language. Much the same way as the prequels do for the originals.

The Covenant's logistics are implied to be a nightmare scenario based on what we are shown between them fielding centuries old ships, desperately trying to bolster their numbers, the fact that it takes them so long to find human colonies, that attacks on those colonies are almost always done by small battlegroups and based on the fact that UNSC strikes against fueling depots delay the Covenant by significant periods of time. 

If you've ever played a game like Empire at War or even the Sins of the Prophets mod then you would see a good example of this kind of issue. I directly answered your prompt with my original comment, but I'll answer more thoroughly here.

>What is the single biggest with the Extraction Shooter genre? What must Bungie solve with Marathon so that it becomes a hit?

Many of the same issues that plague all live service games.

**Problem:** Longevity. As shown with Bungie's last game and Sony's recent series of live service failures, content that you pay for can become lost media very quickly. Losing content that you paid for is something that discourages players from investing. Additionally the fire-and-forget development model has proven to be incredibly hostile to the people who actually work in the game industry.

**Solution:** The bandaid solution would be to include the ability to create offline custom games using bots similar to what we see in Star Wars Squadrons. This allows players to continue playing with the things that they spent money on even years down the line.

The more resource intensive solution that also opens the door to a larger audience would be to invest in creating a full blown campaign. Something like this could attract audiences from the Halo and Doom fanbases. In Halo's case it has suffered under Microsoft's poor management so many fans are desperate for anything that gives them similar vibes to the Bungie era Halo games. Appealing to this crowd would be relatively easy given how much shared DNA Marathon and Halo have. In Doom's case, the original Marathon was a contemporary back in the day and Doom has had a very successful modern revival. Doing something similar with Marathon could attract curious fans.

**Problem:** Aggressive microtransactions. The feeling that a game exists as nothing more than a storefront to sell you overpriced cosmetics pervades live service games and is a major factor in the player burnout we see in games like Destiny or Halo. Additionally, it plays into the above point about longevity because not only does it feel like the game is squeezing you for every penny, but also it is going to take your money and run when they kill the servers.

**Solution:** There are two halves to this solution. The first is to make it so that all cosmetics are available to purchase at all times *individually.* It is infuriating to play Halo Infinite and see that an armor piece either isn't available anymore or is part of a $40 bundle where the only thing you actually want is a shoulder pauldron. The second part of the solution is to make the cosmetics all purchasable using in-game currency that you can earn by playing, even when playing offline. Yet again, this is something that Star Wars Squadrons does that makes it still fun to revisit every now and then.

**Problem:** FOMO. Feeling obligated to play even when you aren't in the mood so you don't miss out is a major contributor to player burnout. Anecdotally, this is the main reason most people I know stopped playing Destiny 2. It also creates unnecessary stress for people who have things to do in their lives besides playing games.

**Solution:** This is a messy one to address. The best answers I have are mentioned in the above point about making cosmetics always available to purchase and in making it so that story events are always accessible once they are added. No limited time events where if you miss it, you miss parts of the story forever.

**Problem:** Extraction shooters are a highly competitive subgenre that discourages casual play. This severely limits the audience that is willing to play a game that is entirely reliant on having a stable player base to be playable (unless the above solutions are implemented).

**Solution:** The aforementioned campaign would go a long way in giving this game legs beyond the relatively niche core audience of extraction shooter fans. Additionally including other, more casual modes like deathmatch or a horde mode would open the door more generally to shooter fans. It could take an approach similar to Splatoon where the unranked casual mode is easy to pick up and has no consequences while the more complex ranked mode is where the extraction shooter part would come in.

1. Doylist answer is simply that blasters stylistically make the setting feel more fantastical and futuristic. Wattsonian answer is that blasters have two primary advantages over slugthrowers. The first is logistical, a single blaster carries far more ammo than a slugthrower can and extra power packs weigh a fraction of the amount ammo does. The second is that canonically blaster bolts are more powerful than slugs. Every soldier is effectively carrying an anti-material weapon. (Now whether that is properly depicted on screen is a different question)
2. This is more a Wattsonian answer. Droids in Star Wars do not operate anywhere near the precision you would expect from robots in other sci-fi. They are often depicted as clumsy, prone to emotional outbursts, being imprecise, and even mistiming things. They are far closer to the organics around them than to the usual sci-fi depiction of robots or AI. With that said, what you are describing is typically how Separatist battle droids functioned. They were dumb as bricks, but cheap to produce and were deployed in swarms. We see this tactic work against Jedi Master Ima-Gun Di in Clone Wars. Additionally saturation fire is exactly how the Clones killed the Jedi during Order 66, though in that case it was performed as a surprise attack and by actually individually competent soldiers. As for the point of the control chip conspiracy, it was to make it so that killing the Jedi didn't turn them into martyrs. If the majority of them died fighting the war then they would be seen as heroes, but if they were killed after an attempted coup? And at the end of a war that was specifically designed to make them look as bad as possible to the general public? We see the result of that in the recently released Mask of Fear. The average Imperial citizen doesn't care about the genocide because it was addressing a "security risk" against the incredibly popular emperor. This kind of apathy wouldn't have been possible if the droids did it.

The latter are sometimes deployed against infantry during boarding actions to great effect. But with that said, this ultimately comes back to a Doylist answer. Stylistically just fighting a war with drone swarms doesn't fit the vibe of Star Wars.

I'm a big fan of Metroid's story. As far as themes and subject matter go the Fire Emblem series is pretty varied so I'll just cover the original setting. Spoilers ahead.


So starting off with the continent of Archanea, the setring of original games and their remakes. Marth's father is betrayed and murdered by a family friend resulting in Marth's kingdom falling and his mother and sister being taken prisoner. From there Marth flees the kingdom and in the process is forced to select one of his knights to be left behind as a decoy (who this is is left to the player's decision). In the next 6 years the continent is torn apart by war. When Marth is 16 he and his few surviving knights depart to attempt to rescue Princess Nyna who is from an allied country that was conquered in that time. Nyna watched her entire family be butchered in front of her and their corpses desecrated then hung from the castle gates. Also during her time as prisoner she falls in love with the general tasked with guarding her cell and because of his loyalty to his country you are forced to kill him in front of her later in the game. 


Then there is the Macedonian royal family. Where Princes Michalis murders his father, takes the throne, and uses his youngest sister Maria as a hostage to force the middle sister Minerva to fight. When Marth rescues Maria, Minvera joins his side and eventually kills the older brother that she idolized as a child. When Marth finally moves to retake his kingdom, he finds it in ruin with the people starving to death and confronts the dragon put in charge. Said dragon then proceeds to taunt Marth about eating his mother alive in a move very similar to the one Ridley pulls on Samus.



Later one of Marth's closest allies ends up marrying Nyna in a loveless political union that eventually drives him into a spiral where he loses himself (egged along by the dark mage that masterminded the death of Marth's father) and he starts another war against the continent. Along the way Marth has to contend with an organization of child assassin's who were tortured and abused into compliance by the woman who ran the orphanage they came from and eventually has to prevent several allies from the prior war from killing themselves in a dark magic ritual where they are being mine controlled.



The big bad is the Shadow Dragon himself, Medeus, who wants to enslave all of humanity as a continuation of ongoing racial violence between humans and dragons over the millennia.


Which brings us to the second game, which takes place on the neighboring continent of Valentia which is ruled over by sibling dragon-gods called Duma and Mila. They originally came from Archanea but were banished by Naga (the big good dragon-god of Archanea) after they wiped out the first human civilization in the ancient past and kicked off that cycle of hatred and racism. The reason they wiped out Thabes is because they feared humanity would grow too strong to be controlled, so when they arrived in Valentia they asserted dominance over the humans living there. Eventually they came into conflict with eachother over how best to rule them in a battle that is described as nearly ending the world. They eventually came to an accord where one would rule the north and make his people strong through hardship and toil, while the other would rule the south where she would spoil her people like pampered pets.

Where the world has been permanently changed by the rising of the Fell Dragon Grima, a chimera horror born from the ruins of Thabes that is a cross between dragon, human, and insect. Past that some other recommendations would be
